newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh cyclone victims need immediate help.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh cyclone victims need immediate help.

text.p: More than 1.5 million people left homeless in Bangladesh by a cyclone that reportedly killed hundreds need shelters immediately, not food or clothing, relief officials said on Wednesday.
"The immediate need is housing materials for the victims, prices of which have gone up by over 50 percent," said Gawhar Nayeem of Oxfam.

Nayeem said a meeting of U.N. representatives, aid agencies and foreign ambassadors, who visited cyclone-hit areas on Wednesday, felt the "extent of damage or loss of lives was not even five percent of that of the 1991 cyclone."
He was referring to the country's worst storm in 1991, which killed at least 138,000 people and left millions homeless.
"They saw life as usual in most areas with few exceptions where 50 percent or more houses had been fully or partially destroyed," Nayeem told Reuters, adding he had attended the meeting himself.
He said relief operations had yet to get into full swing.
Low-lying Bangladesh is prone to devastation from cyclones.

Officials, police and the Cyclone Preparedness Centre (CPC) in Chittagong said on Wednesday afternoon that the latest death toll of 121 might rise, with some 1,500 fishermen still missing in the Bay of Bengal.
"Many of them may not return eventually," an official in Cox's Bazar said.
"The death count may go up but we don't expect any dramatic rise," one CPC official said.
The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs in Geneva said on Wednesday that the cyclone had killed at least 200 people.
It also reported widespread destruction of houses after the cyclone roared in from the Bay of Bengal on Monday, battering coastal areas with 200 kph (125 mph) winds and a tidal surge.

A department statement said the Bangladesh government was trying to assess the damage in disaster-hit areas. U.N. relief officials would take part in an airborne survey mission with donor representatives on Thursday.
Officials said on Tuesday night nearly 400,000 houses had been damaged and 15,000 cattle killed. More than 1.5 million people were made homeless or otherwise affected.
"We are making a full assessment of the losses, which may take a week or more. But so far it looks like the extent (of damage) is within a manageable limit," an official said.
"However, many areas remain out of reach and may have suffered wider damage," said the official supervising relief operations in southeastern areas of the country that bore the brunt of the storm.
The government has launched a huge rescue and relief operation in areas devastated on Monday. Army, naval and police units joined thousands of volunteers fanning out across the coastal regions.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Wednesday flew to affected areas she could not reach on her first trip on Tuesday.
Hasina said Bangladesh should increase the number of cyclone shelters on the coast from 700 to at least 2,000 to cope with similar disasters in future, one official said.
"We are not appealing for international help but of course will welcome (it) if anyone offers...," Hasina said on Tuesday. She urged Bangladeshis to donate generously to a relief fund.
Newspapers said the cyclone had killed between 350 and 500 people, and at least 5,000 were injured. The official figure for injuries was "thousands".
Nayeem who has worked for Oxfam since before the 1991 cyclone said this year's "minimal loss of lives and property" was due to several reasons.

"The first was that storm warning and evacuation of likely victims was conducted well in advance. There were more shelters than in 1991 and people got enough time to prepare themselves (for the impending disaster)."
Agriculture officials said the country's rice crop largely escaped damage.
